extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim language has proper antecedent basis under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112 (second paragraph), including when to make rejections, when to suggest corrections, and when claim language is sufficiently definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim indefiniteness from lack of antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear (e.g., referring to 'said lever' or 'the lever' where no earlier recitation or limitation of a lever appears, or where two different levers are recited earlier making it unclear which is meant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: referring to 'said aluminum lever' when only 'a lever' was recited earlier is indefinite because it is uncertain which lever is referenced. If two different levers are recited earlier, later recitation of 'said lever' is unclear. Case citation: In re Packard, 751 F.3d 1307. Examiner should identify such ambiguities as indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable ascertainability by a person skilled in the art negates indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is not indefinite if its scope would be reasonably ascertainable by those skilled in the art, even absent explicit antecedent wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If skilled artisans can reasonably determine what the claim refers to, lack of explicit antecedent wording does not render the claim indefinite. Example: 'controlled stream of fluid' provided reasonable antecedent basis for 'the controlled fluid' (Ex parte Porter, 25 USPQ2d 1144). Examiners must assess whether the claim language, taken as a whole, apprises one of ordinary skill of its scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent characteristics in an element can supply antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherent components or characteristics of a recited element are considered to have antecedent basis in that element's recitation (e.g., 'the outer surface of said sphere' does not require an earlier recitation that the sphere has an outer surface).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical or physical inherent properties may provide antecedent basis (Bose Corp. v. JBL, Inc., 274 F.3d 1354: recitation of 'an ellipse' provided antecedent basis for 'an ellipse having a major diameter' because a major diameter is an inherent characteristic). Examiners should recognize inherent features when assessing antecedent problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner should suggest constructive corrections for antecedent problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Antecedent problems are typically drafting oversights and examiners should identify and suggest corrections in a positive, constructive way so minor problems can be easily corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner's role is to ensure claim language complies with statutory requirements but to expend effort proportionately—identify minor antecedent oversights for applicant correction. However, even if correctable, indefiniteness is not automatically unobjectionable merely because it could have been fixed (In re Hammack, 427 F.2d 1384).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms lacking antecedent basis in the specification are not necessarily indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of a term in the specification as an antecedent does not by itself render the claim indefinite; there is no requirement that claim wording must match the specification verbatim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants have latitude in defining the invention by their chosen claim terms so long as those terms define the invention with reasonable clarity and precision. Examiners should evaluate whether the claim terms, even if not mirrored in the spec, still convey definite scope to skilled artisans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional elements in the claim body absent from the preamble do not per se cause indefiniteness—consider the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is not per se indefinite simply because the body of the claim recites elements not appearing in the preamble; the totality of claim limitations and their interaction must be considered to determine whether the claim apprises one of ordinary skill of its scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the claim in its entirety to determine the inventor's contribution to the art and whether the notice function of 35 U.S.C. 112 is satisfied. Example: In re Larsen—preamble omitted a linear member that appeared in the body; the court reversed the examiner's rejection after finding the claim as a whole was sufficiently definite.
